# Color Scripting

## Purpose

Decide what color and tone do in this comic before any page is generated.
The plan covers the overall strategy (black and white, a limited palette,
or full color), the rule for any spot color, and how light and dark move
from scene to scene. Written down, it stops each page from choosing its own
palette.

## Use When

- Writing the style bible, once the line and rendering are settled.
- The project uses a spot color and its rule has not been stated.
- Pages of one scene come back with different palettes or different
  amounts of black.
- A new scene or time of day needs its place in the progression.

## Inputs

- `production/project.yaml`: `color_mode`, `spot_colors`, `deliverables`.
- `production/style/style-bible.md` and the look master.
- Scene files: `location`, `time_of_day`, and each scene's place in the
  story.
- Location files, for light sources per time-of-day state.
- Turning points from `narrative-structure`.

## Process

1. Read `color_mode` and confirm the strategy with the art-director. Each
   strategy has a cost. Monochrome puts all separation on value and shape.
   A limited palette gives each color a job. Full color needs fixed local
   colors for every character and place.
2. For `monochrome`, plan values. State how many tones exist besides black
   and white (often none), what is black by rule (the night sky, Mara's
   coat), and how figures separate from grounds: light on dark or dark on
   light, decided per scene.
3. For `limited`, name two to four colors with hex values and give each a
   job: one for night exteriors, one for interiors, one for memory. State
   which things take which color and what stays black, white, or paper.
4. For `full_color`, fix local colors first: skin, hair, and each outfit
   per character, the main surfaces per location. Then give each scene a
   dominant hue, a secondary, and an accent, with hex anchors and a ceiling
   on saturation. Scene light tints local color; it does not replace it.
5. Write the spot color rule. Each entry in `project.spot_colors` has a
   `name`, a `hex`, and a `use` that assigns one named color to one named
   thing: "signal red: flare light only". The rule covers what takes the
   color and, by exclusion, that nothing else does. List the pages where
   it appears.
6. Lay out the tonal progression. Make one row per scene: how dark the
   pages are overall, how hard the contrast is, and where the lightest and
   darkest pages fall. Tie the largest shift to a turning point, so that
   the change in tone happens when the story changes.
7. Add page-level notes only for exceptions: the page where the spot color
   first appears, a flash that inverts the values, a memory in a second
   tone.
8. Keep places consistent. The same location at the same time of day keeps
   the same palette. It changes when `time_of_day` changes or when a
   written reason says so.
9. Test legibility. Convert the plan to grey in your head or on a test
   page: characters still separate from backgrounds and from each other.
   No identity depends on telling red from green. Balloons and captions
   keep strong contrast against every scene palette.
10. If `deliverables` includes `print`, note where saturated screen colors
    will dull in CMYK and choose anchors that survive it
    (`rules/paged/print-specs.md`).
11. Write `production/style/color-script.md` with the strategy, the spot
    rule, the scene table with one row per scene ID, and the exceptions. Update
    `spot_colors` in `project.yaml`. Palette statements that apply to every
    page go into the style block before it is frozen.

## Outputs

- `production/style/color-script.md`.
- `spot_colors` (and a confirmed `color_mode`) in `production/project.yaml`.
- Palette wording for `production/style/style-block.txt`, supplied to
  `visual-style-development` before the freeze.

## Quality Bar

- The color script names the strategy and it matches `project.color_mode`.
- Every spot color has a `use` naming exactly one thing, and the script
  lists the pages where it appears.
- Every scene in the issue has a row in the progression table.
- Every named color has a hex value.
- Two scenes in the same location and time of day share a palette, or the
  script states why they differ.
- The plan passes the grey test: no pair of characters relies on hue alone.

## Common Failure Modes

- A spot color with no rule. Red starts as the flare, then turns up on a
  scarf and a sign, and by the last page it marks nothing.
- "Monochrome" understood as greyscale rendering. Soft grey gradients
  replace the black shapes the style bible asked for.
- The same amount of black on every page, so night, interior, and climax
  all weigh the same.
- Palette chosen page by page. The deck is blue-black on page 2 and
  green-black on page 3.
- Scene tint overriding local color until two characters' coats match.
- Characters separated only by hue, which fails in a black-and-white
  edition and for color-blind readers.
- Dark caption boxes over dark panels.
- Screen-bright accents that go flat in print.

## Notes

A monochrome comic still has a color script; it is a script of values. The
plan feeds `pixel-review`, which checks pages against it under the
`style_fidelity` gate. The rule is `rules/visual/visual-language.md`.
